To the north is a 20-mile region around the segment of the Yellowstone River that passes through Rosebud. The southern tip of the county is viable due to its proximity to the tongue river reservoir to the southwest, which flows north to empty into the Yellowstone and could potentially provide cooling water for a reactor. With regard to restrictions, there does not appear to be significant risk of landslides, fault lines, seismic activity, or flooding in the region. Instead, the limitations are logistical in nature, with steep terrain and the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation precluding most of the southern half of the county. Moving on to the suitability maps for a small modular reactor in Table M.R2, very little seems to change with the reduced water requirement. The only criteria that meaningfully alters the viability is that of slope, which greatly increases the amount of suitable land in the aforementioned regions. With the removal of the cooling water requirement, the suitability maps for dry-cooled SMR technology in Table M.R3 show large swaths of viability north of the Cheyenne Reservation. These seem to increase in continuity moving north, corresponding with the flatter terrain shows in the slope criteria map. No other criteria appear to present significant restrictions to siting suitability. With regard to siting for data centers, Table M.R4 shows nearly no meaningful restrictions in Rosebud County. Only two criteria conflict with a siting decision in any area of the county: locations of wetlands and open water, and slope. Given the greater tolerance for slope, this obstruction is minimal.
